proposedchanges.description_long:
Amnesty International published its report, “President Trump’s First 100 Days: Attacks on Human Rights, Cruelty and Chaos,” on April 30, 2025. It reviewed domestic and international policies and argued that their effects overlapped. Examples included restrictions on asylum and mass deportations, detention of Palestinian student Mahmoud Khalil after protests at Columbia University, actions affecting press freedom, anti-trans policies, and cuts to foreign assistance. Amnesty’s executive director described the cumulative effect as a broad assault on human rights and the institutions that protect them.

Amnesty also discussed court compliance, racial equity, and withdrawals from international bodies. These examples show the report’s breadth across policy areas. Its claims about legality, authoritarianism, and cumulative harm are Amnesty’s assessment, not court findings. The report does not claim that every policy had the same effect or that its publication resolved legal disputes. Its concluding warning was that the combined measures threatened rights and the institutions intended to protect them during the administration’s first 100 days.

evidencebasis: The packet and latest description attribute the first-100-days review and its named examples to Amnesty. The replacement removes internal commentary and keeps the organization’s judgments attributed. The Amnesty URL remains in source_urls.
notes: The title and medium already identify the review and distinguish Amnesty’s assessment from a court judgment.

proposedchanges.title: At Least 16 Epstein Files Disappeared From DOJ Public Webpage
proposedchanges.description_short: At Least 16 Epstein Files Disappeared From DOJ Public Webpage
proposedchanges.description_long: The Justice Department published a batch of Epstein-related files on December 19, 2025. Less than a day later, at least 16 files were no longer accessible on its public webpage, the Associated Press reported. One missing item was a photograph showing Donald Trump, Jeffrey Epstein, Melania Trump, and Ghislaine Maxwell; other missing material included images of paintings. DOJ did not answer AP’s questions about why the files disappeared or whether the removals were intentional. The department later said on X that photographs and other material would continue to be reviewed and redacted as it received new information. That statement did not account for the specific missing files. The public-facing change raised questions about transparency in a release that had already drawn scrutiny, but the reporting does not identify who made the changes or prove that government records were destroyed, altered, or removed from custody. AP documented missing items on the webpage and an incomplete explanation; it did not report a forensic chain-of-custody failure.

evidencebasis: The packet reports at least 16 files disappeared from the DOJ webpage. The latest long description identifies the file-release timing, photograph, DOJ’s general statement, and limits on what the report establishes. The AP URL remains in source_urls.
notes: The proposed copy separates missing public access from destruction, alteration, or removal from government custody.
